title: Great by hearsay
hookLine: suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe: everyone calls You great from hearing, but only one who has seen knows (Asa, ang 9)
last: SO DAR — THE DOOR AT DUSK.

lines: A BOY WHO HAS HEARD ABOUT THE SEA.
HE REPEATS IT: THE SEA IS HUGE.
THEN HE SEES IT, AND GOES QUIET.
cards: A boy from a village far inland grows up hearing about the sea. His uncle has been. The ocean is huge, the uncle says, bigger than all of Punjab, salty, loud, it never stops moving.
The boy repeats it to his friends: the sea is huge. He's right. But he doesn't know it.
Years later, he steps off a bus on the coast and walks to the edge of the water, and he goes completely quiet. He never says the sea is huge again.

teach.b: The second shabad of Rehras, Guru Nanak again, in Raag Asa, begins: suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe. Hearing, everyone calls You great.

teach.h: ONLY ONE WHO HAS SEEN CAN SAY.
teach.b: And then, in paraphrase: but how great You are, only someone who has seen can say. That's a startling way to open an evening prayer.
It admits that talk about God can be hearsay: things we were told and repeated, secondhand. Guru Nanak doesn't mock it. Everyone says You're great, and they're right.
But hearing is not the same as seeing. Then the shabad does something even more honest. It says those who did see couldn't describe it either.
Your worth can't be estimated, it says, and can't be spoken.

teach.h: THOSE WHO SAW WERE LEFT SPEECHLESS.
teach.b: Those who tried to describe You were absorbed into You. The refrain calls out: my great Master, deep and profound, an ocean of virtue, nobody knows how vast You are.

All the meditators met and meditated, it says; all the appraisers met and appraised; the scholars and teachers tried; and none of them could tell even a sliver. So the shabad leaves us between two things.
Hearsay isn't enough, and seeing leaves you speechless. Like the boy at the sea.

teach.h: HEARING BEGINS; SEEING IS THE PATH.
teach.b: Some readers set this beside the Japji's suniai pauris: hearing as a real beginning, and seeing, knowing for yourself, as where the path goes. For the evening, the question is simple.
What, today, did you actually see, not just hear about?

how: Suni vaddaa is the second shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; some Sikh teachers draw from it the reading that hearing about the Divine is a beginning, and knowing for oneself is the goal.

o: great, from hearing: praise on hearsay
a well-known teacher, known by reputation
the great sound heard in deep meditation

games.q: the second shabad — tap the pairs.
p: deep, profound, an ocean of virtue

s: the shabad mocks people who call God great from hearsay
it says they're right; it only says hearing isn't the same as seeing.
the shabad says those who saw could not describe it
those who tried were absorbed; no one could tell even a sliver.
this is the second shabad of Rehras
it follows So Dar, also by Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa.

games.q: everyone you know calls something great, but you've only heard about it. what does the shabad say about knowing the Lord's greatness?
o: trust the crowd: if everyone says it, you know it.
only one who has seen can say, and even they fall silent.
nobody should ever talk about it.
games.why: Guru Nanak says hearing is not seeing, and then admits that those who saw were left speechless: the Lord's worth can't be told.

practice: Find one thing from today or yesterday that you saw or felt for yourself, a kindness, a sky, a moment of peace, a fear that passed: not something you read about, something you were there for.
Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, I saw, I felt, and sit with it quietly, the way the boy stood at the water. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: Suni vaddaa, hearing, great: everyone calls the Lord great from hearing; only one who has seen knows, and even they can't describe it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: suni vaddaa, hearing, great; the opening of the second shabad of Rehras.

carryVoice: Your line: seen, not heard. Hearing is where it begins, not where it ends. That's today.

sources.ref: Asa M1, suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe, Ang 9
